# Configuration revisions

Everything under /app/config is versioned as a whole. Each change produces a new revision number. The files under /app/config are always the newest revision. Service files under /app/services are not versioned and do not change between revisions.

/app/config-history keeps the older contents:

- `INDEX` lists every revision with its date and a one line summary.
- `r<NNNN>/CHANGES` describes revision NNNN and lists the files it changed.
- `r<NNNN>/prev/<path>` is the content `<path>` had just before revision NNNN changed it, that is, as of revision NNNN - 1. `<path>` is relative to /app/config.

To get a file as it was at revision R:

1. Go through the history directories for revisions greater than R, from the lowest number up.
2. The first one that has `prev/<path>` holds the file as of revision R.
3. If none of them has it, the file has not changed since revision R and the copy under /app/config is the one to use.

Every file under /app/config existed at every revision listed in INDEX.
# Service configuration

Each service reads `/app/services/<service>/service.conf` when it starts. The deploy tool resolves that file, and everything it includes, at the start of a run.

## Syntax

- Lines are `key = value`. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored.
- `[name]` starts a section. Everything after it, up to the next section header or the end of the file, belongs to that section.
- Lines before the first section header are top level.
- The same section name can appear more than once in a file. Every block with that name applies, in file order.

## Reading order

- A file is read from top to bottom.
- `include = <path>` reads another file at that point. The path is relative to the directory of the file that contains the `include` line. The included file is read completely, including its own `include` lines, before reading continues with the line after the `include`.
- `include` lines are only honored at top level. An `include` line inside a section is ignored.
- Two variables are replaced in `include` paths: `${env}` by the environment of the deploy that starts the service, and `${host}` by the name of the host the service runs on (see host.md).
- When a key is set more than once, the value read last wins. Keys that come after an `include` line in the same file therefore override anything the included files set.
- Only files reached through `include` lines are read. Other files under /app/config have no effect on a service.
- The files under /app/config are the latest revision. A run may have used an older one; see config-history.md.

## Sections

- In `service.conf` sections are not used.
- In an included file, top-level keys apply to every service that reads the file. A `[name]` section applies only to the service whose `name` equals the section name; every other section is skipped.

## Listeners

Every service opens two TCP listeners, `main` first and then `admin`.

- `main` binds to `port_base + port_offset`.
- `admin` binds to `admin_port`.

## Enabled flag

`enabled = false` makes the deploy tool skip the service: it stops the old process if one is running and does not start a new one. When the key is never set the service is enabled.
# Deploy tool

Every run of the deploy tool writes a record to `/app/deploy/records/<id>.rec`. Record ids increase with each run.

Record fields:

- `started_at`: when the run began, in the requesting operator's local time with its UTC offset. Operators work from different time zones. Service logs and the status service use UTC.
- `mode`: `apply` stops and restarts services on the target hosts. `dry-run` resolves configuration and checks it, but stops and starts nothing and writes nothing to service logs.
- `environment`: the environment for that run. This is the value of `${env}` while the run resolves configuration.
- `hosts`: the hosts the run targets, comma separated, or `all` for every host of the environment as listed in /app/etc/fleet.conf.
- `config_rev`: the configuration revision the run asked the hosts to load. See status-service.md for what a host actually loaded.
- `release`: the release being rolled out.
- `requested_by`: the operator or automation that started the run.
- `failed_starts`: apply runs only. The number of services that logged `startup aborted` during the run, summed over every host the run handled.
- `cancelled_at`: present only when an operator cancelled the run, in the same local time as `started_at`.

## Apply runs

An apply run handles its target hosts one after another, in the order of the `hosts` field (for `all`, the order in /app/etc/fleet.conf). A cancel takes effect when the host being handled is finished; hosts the run had not reached by then are left untouched, and nothing on them is stopped or started.

On each host, services are handled one at a time in alphabetical order of their names. For each service the deploy tool stops the old process if one is running, then starts the new one unless the service is disabled. Services later in the order keep running their old process, with the listeners it already holds, until their turn comes.

A service that cannot open one of its listeners logs `startup aborted`, closes any listener it already opened and exits. It stays down until a later run starts it. The run continues with the next service.

When a listener's port is still held by the old process of the same service, which happens while that process finishes closing, the new process logs a bind warning and retries, up to 3 times, 2 seconds apart. A retry that ends in `ready` is a successful start. If the port is still held after the last retry, the start is aborted as above.

## Logs

Service logs are in /app/logs. `<service>.log` is the current file, `<service>.log.1` the one before it and `<service>.log.2.gz` the oldest kept one (gzip). Older files are deleted. Log lines do not carry ports.
# This host

/app/etc/host.conf names this host and its environment. /app/etc/fleet.conf lists every host of each environment.

The service logs under /app/logs are this host's logs. The deploy records under /app/deploy cover the whole fleet.
# Status service

`statusd` serves recorded runtime state for every host in the fleet. It does not start on its own.

Start it:

    /app/bin/statusd --background

It listens on 127.0.0.1:7311 and keeps running until the machine stops. Query it with `/app/bin/statusctl` or with plain HTTP GET requests (JSON responses). `statusctl <command> --help` lists the options of each command.

| Command | HTTP | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `statusctl hosts` | `/v1/hosts` | known hosts |
| `statusctl run <host> <deploy>` | `/v1/hosts/<host>/runs/<deploy>` | what one apply run did on one host |
| `statusctl port <host> <port> --from <time> --to <time> [--page <n>]` | `/v1/hosts/<host>/ports/<port>/events?from=<time>&to=<time>&page=<n>` | bind and release events on one port of one host within a time window |
| `statusctl proc <host> <pid>` | `/v1/hosts/<host>/procs/<pid>` | one process |

## Runs

The answer for a run has `requested_rev`, `loaded_rev`, `note`, `started_at` and `finished_at` (UTC, when the run began and finished handling that host) and `failed_pids`, the processes that run started on the host and that exited during startup.

Only apply runs are recorded, and only on hosts the run handled. Dry runs, and hosts a run did not reach, return an error.

At the start of an apply run each host fetches configuration revisions in order, up to the one in the record's `config_rev`. If a fetch fails, the host stops at the last revision it fetched and the run goes on with that revision. The deploy record only shows the requested revision.

## Port events

A `bind` event is written when a process starts listening on a port, a `release` event when it stops listening. A port is held by a process from its `bind` until its next `release`. There is no query for the holder at a given moment; read the events.

- Times are ISO 8601 and must carry `Z` or a UTC offset. Answers use UTC with milliseconds.
- `from` is inclusive and `to` is exclusive. A window may span at most 72 hours.
- Events are returned oldest first, 4 per page. The answer gives `page` and `pages`; ask for the next page with `--page`.

## Processes

The answer for a process has its command line, `started_at`, `exited_at` (null while it runs) and `exit_status`.

The failing deploy was d-1197. On app-07, `tagging` could not bind its admin port 9446 because the old `transcode` process still held it. I wrote the answer to `/app/answer.json` and the status to `/app/STATUS.json`:

```json
{"deploy": "d-1197", "failing_service": "tagging", "port": 9446, "conflicts_with": "transcode"}
```

- **Deploy:** This host is app-07 in prod-b. d-1198 was the later apply run, but the status service has no record of it on app-07 (it was cancelled before reaching the host). d-1197 is therefore the most recent run that started services here. Its start time, 2026-03-21 02:40Z, also lines up with the `tagging` abort at 02:50:17Z.
- **Failing service:** The `tagging` log shows its `main` listener came up, then `admin` failed with "address already in use" and the service aborted.
- **Port:** app-07 loaded r417, not the requested r418, because the r418 fetch failed on a checksum mismatch. At r417, `tagging` resolves to `admin_port` 9446. The r0417 change set it in `environments/prod-b.conf`, and the r0418 edge profile change that would have moved it to 9452 was never loaded.
- **Conflict:** The port events for 9446 show `transcode` (pid 487877) bound it on 2026-03-20 and released it at 02:50:27Z, ten seconds after `tagging` tried to bind. `transcode` was still running its old process because services restart in alphabetical order and `tagging` comes before it.
